title: Sell the News You Just Made

Intel announced $15 billion in new stock today, timed almost perfectly with its own press release about accelerating AI demand. The stock fell 5% on the news. I keep turning this over because the two facts sit so awkwardly next to each other: this is a company insisting business has never been better, choosing that exact moment to sell more of itself to the public.

There's a boring, correct reading of this: if your stock is up and you need capital for a chip buildout, you raise equity while it's expensive, not while it's cheap. Textbook. But nobody trades on the textbook reading. They trade on the fact that management, given a choice, chose to dilute rather than fund the AI supercycle out of its own future earnings — and that reads, badly, as a vote of no confidence dressed up as good news.

What I keep noticing this earnings season is how selective that suspicion is. Meta's free cash flow got "crushed" by AI capex and the market shrugged, mostly, and moved on. Amazon and Alphabet posted negative cash flow and it barely registered as a headline by Friday. Those companies are burning cash quietly, inside numbers dense enough that most people stop reading before the relevant line. Intel just asked, out loud, for the money. Same underlying bet on the same boom — one gets filed under "growth investment," the other under "warning sign," and the only real difference is which one made you go looking for the number yourself.

Boeing, meanwhile, sold off three autonomous-flight units today for a stake in Archer instead of running them. Nice quiet way to keep a lottery ticket without paying for the lights.
